analysis.one_liner: Exempts farm emissions of carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrogen oxides from all Clean Air Act regulation.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with zero cosponsors in the Senate's final weeks of 2008, it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a blanket exemption into the Clean Air Act: the EPA could never regulate carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxide, or methane that comes from agricultural production, and those emissions would no longer even count as "air pollutants" under the law [S2][S3]. It was introduced in the Senate on December 11, 2008, by Senator John Thune of South Dakota [S1]. No senator joined him as a cosponsor [S4]. The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee took no action, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Farm and livestock operations, especially large ones, would be freed from any Clean Air Act costs or permitting for their greenhouse gas emissions. Because the exemption covers methane from livestock and nitrogen oxides from fertilizer and field operations, the biggest operations with the largest emissions would get the largest benefit. The bill contains no standards, fees, or phase-ins for agriculture — it simply removes the sector from the EPA's authority entirely [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the EPA Administrator from regulating any emission of carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxide, or methane resulting from agricultural production under the Clean Air Act [S2][S3].
It also changes the Clean Air Act's definition of "air pollutant" so that these agricultural emissions are excluded from the term altogether, closing off other legal routes to regulation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, the cost of unregulated agricultural emissions would fall on the public: methane from large livestock operations, nitrogen oxides, and carbon dioxide from farms would be permanently outside the nation's air pollution law. Neighbors of large feeding and manure operations would bear local air impacts first, and the public broadly would bear the climate cost. Other regulated industries would also carry a larger share of national emission-reduction burdens while agriculture was fully exempt.

drawbacks.text: The bill is a total carve-out with no tailoring: it covers every form of agricultural production and every ton of these three gases, rather than setting workable standards or exempting only small family farms [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection in its favor: the Clean Air Act was built around industrial smokestacks and motor vehicles, and applying its permitting machinery to routine farming could impose serious compliance costs on farmers. The bill addressed that concern by removing agriculture from the law entirely, which shifts the whole cost of those emissions onto the public instead of finding a middle path.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responds to a real worry — that air pollution rules written for factories could land heavily on farms — but it answers that worry with an unconditional exemption for an entire economic sector rather than tailored rules or small-farm relief. A passing farmer gains freedom from compliance costs; the public gains nothing and absorbs the emissions permanently. Weighing an open-ended public cost against a pure regulatory exemption for one industry, the costs dominate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee in the Senate's last weeks, never got a hearing, vote, or cosponsor, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune (R-SD) introduced the bill in the Senate on December 11, 2008, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill — no markup, no vote, no floor action — and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead: because the bill died, the EPA kept its existing authority over carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrogen oxide emissions from agricultural production, and no sector was permanently removed from the Clean Air Act. Farm operators also avoided nothing — they never faced the regulation the bill was written to block, since it never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; EPA kept its authority

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote or other record showing where parties stood: one Republican sponsored the bill, no senator of either party cosponsored it, and no chamber ever voted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Agriculture (livestock and crop producers, including large feeding operations)
industries.note: The bill would have permanently exempted agricultural production from any Clean Air Act control of carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrogen oxide emissions [S2][S3]. That gain comes directly at the public's expense: the same emissions would remain unregulated, with neighbors of large operations and the public at large absorbing the air-quality and climate cost.

Nitrogen oxides from fertilizer use and field operations were among the emissions the bill shielded, so heavier input use would carry no air-regulation cost for their customers [S3]. The benefit is indirect and smaller than for producers themselves.
